subject: zoology_2
question_text: What is DNA fingerprinting? Mention its applications.

verification.note: Sourced from 'My Baby Bullet-Q — Senior Inter Zoology' (Star-Q Pass Track Series, Sri Publishers, 2022), book p.26, LAQ 10. The printed exam years are the book's claim, reproduced here as appearances. Zoology-II holds only ONE source book in the corpus, so the two-book union check is structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is our reading of the question and is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

steps.label: What it is
steps.why: Every person's DNA differs slightly, so the pattern of fragments it gives is as individual as a fingerprint.
common_mistakes: Saying it reads the whole genome. It reads a pattern of repeats.
Leaving out the other name, DNA typing.
steps.memory_tip: DNA fingerprinting is also called DNA typing.
steps.margin_note: Definition, other name and uses first.
lines: DNA fingerprinting, or genetic
fingerprinting, is a method of identifying
individuals by the particular structure of
their DNA. It is also called DNA typing.
It is used for maternity and paternity
testing and for forensic work.
DNA can be obtained from any tissue or
fluid of the body, and even from buried
tissues and bones.

steps.label: Why it works
steps.why: Almost all our DNA is shared, so only the few sequences that differ between people can identify anyone.
common_mistakes: Saying everyone's DNA is completely different. Over 99% is identical.
steps.memory_tip: 99% the same; the repeats, the VNTRs, are what differ.
steps.margin_note: Name VNTRs and Jeffreys. Both are marked.
lines: More than 99% of the 3 billion base pairs
are identical in all individuals.
But no two people have the same DNA
sequence, other than identical twins.
The sequences peculiar to an individual are
called variable number tandem repeats,
or VNTRs.
The technique was developed by Jeffreys
from the myoglobin of muscle.

steps.label: Obtaining and cutting
steps.why: The DNA must be cut at fixed sites, or the fragment pattern would differ from run to run and could not be compared.
common_mistakes: Naming the wrong enzyme. Restriction endonucleases do the cutting.
steps.memory_tip: Obtain, then cut with restriction endonucleases.
steps.margin_note: Number the steps. There are six.
lines: 1. Obtaining DNA: DNA is taken from blood,
saliva, hair roots or semen. Copies can be
made by cloning and DNA amplification.
2. Fragmenting DNA: restriction
endonucleases cut the DNA into smaller
fragments at specific sites.

steps.label: Separating and denaturing
steps.why: Smaller fragments move further through the gel, so the fragments sort themselves by size into a pattern of bands.
common_mistakes: Saying larger pieces travel further. Smaller pieces do.
Leaving out that the strands must be separated before probing.
steps.memory_tip: Small pieces run far; alkali splits the two strands.
steps.margin_note: Say which way the fragments move.
lines: 3. Separation by electrophoresis: the
fragments are applied at one end of an
agarose gel plate and an electric current
is applied. The fragments travel across the
gel, and smaller pieces travel farther.
4. Denaturing DNA: alkaline chemicals
separate the two strands of DNA.

steps.label: Blotting
steps.why: The gel is fragile, so the pattern is transferred to a tough nylon sheet before anything further is done to it.
common_mistakes: Naming Northern or Western blotting. For DNA it is Southern blotting.
Leaving out the name of the process.
steps.margin_note: The name Southern blotting carries the mark.
lines: 5. Blotting: a thin nylon membrane is
placed over the DNA fragments on the plate
and covered by a paper towel. The towel
absorbs moisture and the DNA strands are
transferred to the nylon membrane.

lines.text: This process is called Southern blotting

steps.label: Probes and hybridisation
steps.why: The probe pairs only with the sequence it matches, so it marks exactly the fragments of interest and nothing else.
common_mistakes: Making the probe double stranded. It is a single complementary strand.
steps.memory_tip: A radioactive single strand finds its partner and sticks.
steps.margin_note: Say what holds the probe on: hydrogen bonds.
lines: 6. Using probes: radioactive probes are
used. A probe is a complementary single
strand of the sample under study. It
attaches to the sample strand by hydrogen
bonds.
After the probe hybridises, the excess
probe is washed off. A photographic film is
placed on the membrane holding the DNA
hybrids.

steps.label: Exposure on film
steps.why: The radioactive label darkens the film wherever a fragment lies, so the invisible pattern becomes a picture.
common_mistakes: Saying the bands are seen directly on the gel.
Leaving out that the pattern of bands IS the fingerprint.
steps.memory_tip: The film shows thick and thin bands: that pattern is the print.
steps.margin_note: One short paragraph closes the procedure.
lines: The radioactive label exposes the film and
forms an image corresponding to specific
DNA bands.
The thick and thin bands form a pattern
which is called the DNA fingerprint.

steps.label: Applications
steps.why: Every use is the same idea applied to a different question: whose DNA is this.
common_mistakes: Giving fewer than four applications when the question asks for them.
Repeating forensic use twice in different words.
steps.memory_tip: Crime, parentage, pedigree, taxonomy, wildlife, migration.
steps.margin_note: Six numbered applications finish the essay.
lines: 1. Forensic analysis: to identify a suspect
in a crime.
2. Medico-legal cases: to establish
paternity or maternity.
3. Pedigree analysis: to study the
inheritance pattern of a gene.
4. Taxonomy: for the study of phylogeny.
5. Conservation of wildlife: by keeping
DNA records.

insider_note: The six steps must be in order and named — obtain, fragment, separate, denature, blot, probe. An answer that describes the idea without the named steps rarely passes half.
